learning_objective: 🎯 Understand and implement Linear Search and Binary Search, recognizing when sorted data enables logarithmic search speeds.

key_vocabulary.definition: The algorithmic process of finding the index or existence of a target element within a data collection.
A sequential search algorithm that checks every element one by one from beginning to end.
A divide-and-conquer search algorithm that repeatedly halves the search interval on a sorted list.

main_concepts.simple_explanation: Traverses the list element by element until the target is found or the list ends. Works on both sorted and unsorted lists. Time Complexity: Best case $O(1)$ (first item is target), Worst/Average case $O(n)$.

STRICT REQUIREMENT: The list MUST be sorted. It calculates the middle index `mid = (low + high) // 2`. If `target == list[mid]`, search finishes. If `target < list[mid]`, search the left half (`high = mid - 1`). If `target > list[mid]`, search the right half (`low = mid + 1`). Time Complexity: Worst case $O(\log_2 n)$.

Linear search is simple and needs no preprocessing, but is far too slow for massive datasets. Binary search requires the dataset to be sorted first, but searches 1,000,000 items in at most 20 comparisons ($2^{20} \approx 10^6$).

exam_tips: 📌 If a question asks you to apply Binary Search, always verify or explicitly state: *'The array is assumed/required to be sorted in ascending order first.'*
📌 When writing Binary Search code, remember integer division for mid: `mid = (low + high) // 2` (do not use single `/`).
📌 In dry-run questions, make a small table tracking `low`, `high`, `mid`, and `list[mid]` values at each step.
quick_recap: ⭐ Binary search reduces the search space by 50% on every comparison.
⭐ The maximum number of comparisons required by Binary Search on $N$ elements is $\lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor + 1$.
⭐ Linear search is the only option when data is unsorted and sorting it would take longer than searching once.
